title: The Hour I Thought She Was Sleeping
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] For most of my childhood, I assumed my mother slept soundly through the night, the way exhausted, overworked women are generally assumed to, having earned an unconsciousness nothing could interrupt.
Narrator: It was only as a restless teenager, wandering the house near dawn during a difficult exam season, that I discovered otherwise entirely, by accident, through a door left slightly ajar.
Narrator: [carefully] She was kneeling, alone, at an hour I'd never once associated with her, murmuring something I couldn't make out and wasn't, I sensed immediately, meant to overhear.
Narrator: I retreated before she noticed me, oddly embarrassed, as though I'd trespassed on something considerably more private than mere prayer, which perhaps I had.

Narrator: [reflective] For years afterward I said nothing, watching for the pattern, and found it nearly every difficult season of our lives, illness, debt, my own reckless adolescent choices she never once mentioned confronting this way.
Narrator: What strikes me now isn't merely her devotion, which I'd have assumed of her regardless, but the sheer discipline of never once converting it into leverage during our daytime arguments.
Narrator: [honestly] She never said I prayed for you last night as though depositing a debt I now owed her compliance for, never wielded that hour as ammunition when we disagreed.
Narrator: I eventually asked her, as an adult, why she'd kept it so entirely separate from how she raised us, expecting some elaborate theological answer I wasn't prepared to receive.
Narrator: [gently] She simply said that a mother's love shouldn't require an audience to remain genuine, and that mentioning the prayers would have quietly turned them into a transaction.
Narrator: I think about that distinction often now, raising my own children, resisting the urge to catalogue my sacrifices aloud whenever gratitude feels overdue or insufficiently expressed.
Narrator: [calmly] She's older now, her nights shorter, her joints less forgiving of the floor, and still, some mornings, I find that same door left slightly ajar, exactly as it always was.

quiz.question: What did the narrator assume about her mother throughout most of her childhood?
options: That she slept soundly through the night, having earned an unbroken rest
That she never slept at all
That she prayed constantly in public
That she was often away from home
quiz.explanation: She assumed her mother slept soundly through the night, like most exhausted, overworked women.
